title: Practice traditions, closed
hook: chant, bow, retreat, pilgrimage, perfections, vows

segments.voice: Yesterday you planned a retreat: a day, a weekend, or longer, somewhere in the coming year. Your line was plan it. Did anything make it onto paper, even a single date with a question mark? Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

Lay this block out on a table like objects from a long trip. A chant sheet in Pali. A page of the Heart Sutra, marked for a wooden drum. The mani, sung. The name of Amitabha, walked around a hall. A bow, from a small nod to the full length of the floor. A long retreat in noble silence, and a sesshin with sore legs and tea at the end. A map of pilgrim roads: Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar, the island of temples, the mountain. The perfections, one a day. Moon days. Vows for others. A funeral chant, a memorial altar, a meal chant, and yesterday's plan. That's a lot to carry home. Today closes the block on practice traditions with one small, honest step: pick up one thing from the table.
screen: `CHANT, BOW, RETREAT.` → `PILGRIMAGE, PERFECTIONS, VOWS.` → `PICK UP ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Start with the word the tradition uses for all of this: bhavana. It's often translated meditation, but it's wider than sitting. It means cultivation, bringing something into being, the way a gardener brings up a plant. Chanting is bhavana. So is bowing, giving, keeping a precept on a moon day. Every practice in this block is a different kind of gardening. Next, why one and not all. The Dhammapada has a picture for how good grows, in Max Müller's words: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The verse is about not thinking little of small good acts. A drop doesn't fill a pot. A drop, again and again, does. A month of tasting practices is a sampler. A sampler doesn't fill the pot. One practice, kept, does. Then, how to choose. Some teachers put it simply: start with what you'll actually do. Not the most impressive practice. The one that fits your mornings, your body, your house. A short chant you can say while the kettle boils may grow further than a ten-day retreat you never book. And notice that the schools don't ask you to pick a team. In this block, a Theravada chant sat next to a Zen drum and a Pure Land name, and each was taught on its own terms. Choosing one to deepen isn't a verdict on the others. It's just where your water-drops land for now. Last, the block's close. Over the coming days, the festival year comes round again, starting tomorrow with the full moon of Vesak.
screen: `BHAVANA: BRINGING INTO BEING.` · `A DROP, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `START WITH WHAT YOU'LL DO.` · then, large: `CHOOSE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to choose, if you'd like. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle for a few rounds. Then, slowly, let the practices pass by in your mind: the chant, the bow, the retreat, the pilgrim road, the perfections, the vows. Don't decide with your head yet. Notice which one your attention leans toward, the way a plant leans toward a window. When one stays, let it stay. Rest with it. Picture doing it tomorrow, in your real kitchen or your real chair, for a few minutes. If more than one comes, that's fine. Just keep the first. The bell holds the time.
Practice traditions. Ways Buddhists of different schools cultivate the path: chanting, bowing, retreat, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows. Today's word.
Your line: choose one. Today, write the practice you chose somewhere you'll see it tomorrow morning, and do it once, small. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Buddhists in different schools keep practices such as chanting, bowing, meditation retreats, pilgrimage, the perfections and vows, and some settle on one or two that they keep daily, often with a teacher's guidance.
